short.title: Colossi of Memnon: Hidden Sphinxes Found #Shorts
short.title_plain: Colossi of Memnon: Hidden Sphinxes Found
short.hook: Sphinx fragments with royal inscriptions were found behind the Third Pylon.
script: Sphinx fragments with royal inscriptions were found behind the Third Pylon.
They belong to Amenhotep III's mortuary temple, built 1390–1353 BC.
Three Sekhmet busts and column bases were discovered in the courtyard and hall.
Restoration began in 1998, linking new finds to decades of conservation work.
The findings connect to the temple's architectural sequence that linked the gateway, processional route, and pillared hall.
Were the Colossi always just gate guardians, or part of a grander temple narrative?
Tap the link below for the full case file.
short.description:
Sphinx fragments and Sekhmet busts were found behind the Colossi of Memnon in Luxor, Egypt, linked to Amenhotep III's mortuary temple. The discoveries are part of ongoing restoration work at the site, which once included a full temple complex with pylons, courtyard, and pillared hall. The finds confirm the architectural sequence of the temple entrance and processional road. Source: ad-hoc-news.de, https://www.ad-hoc-news.de/unterhaltung/reisen/egypt-reports-new-finds-at-colossi-of-memnon-on-22-october/70509765

fact_check: The line 'The discoveries reveal the temple's full architectural sequence was once intact' claims certainty not supported by the article. The article says the findings 'connect' with the architectural sequence and that the pieces belong to it, but does not state the full sequence was 'once intact'.

The line 'Were the Colossi always just gate guardians, or part of a grander temple narrative?' introduces speculative questioning about the Colossi's role that the article does not support. The article only describes their location and function as gate guardians, without suggesting a 'grander narrative' or posing such a question.
